package_info.package_manager: n/a (malware binary, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.why_malicious: The RA World ransomware is a Windows malware family that exfiltrates sensitive data, encrypts user files, deletes system backups to prevent recovery, and extorts victims by threatening to leak stolen data. It terminates security and backup processes, drops ransom notes, and uses both TOR and clearnet sites for data leaks.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Stops the following services: sophos, veeam, backup, mepocs, GxVss, GxBlr, GxFWD, GxCVD, GxCIMgr, DefWatch, ccEvtMgr, ccSetMgr, SavRoam, RTVscan, QBFCService, QBIDPService, Intuit.QuickBooks.FCS, QBCFMonitorService, YooBackup, YooIT, zhudongfangyu, stc_raw_agent, VSNAPVSS, VeeamTransportSvc, VeeamDeploymentService, VeeamNFSSvc, PDVFSService, BackupExecVSSProvider, BackupExecAgentAccelerator, BackupExecAgentBrowser, BackupExecDiveciMediaService, BackupExecJobEngine, BackupExecManagementService, BackupExecRPCService, AcrSch2Svc, AcronisAgent, CASAD2DWebSvc, CAARCUpdateSvc.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (initial execution), the code enumerates and forcibly stops a comprehensive list of security, backup, and recovery-related services using Windows API calls, disrupting protection and backup mechanisms to facilitate subsequent malicious actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Terminating a wide range of security and backup services is a deliberate tactic to disable system defenses and ensure ransomware can encrypt files without interference.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not indiscriminately stop unrelated security or backup services, as this undermines system integrity and user protection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or security software may stop their own services for updates or maintenance, but not a broad set of unrelated services simultaneously.
key_indicators: Enumerates and stops multiple unrelated security and backup services
Targets well-known AV, backup, and recovery service names
Uses process control APIs to forcibly terminate services

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Terminates the following processes: synctime.exe, agntsvc.exe, isqlplussvc.exe, xfssvccon.exe, mydesktopservice.exe, ocautoupds.exe, encsvc.exe, firefox.exe, tbirdconfig.exe, mydesktopqos.exe, ocomm.exe, dbeng50.exe, sqbcoreservice.exe, excel.exe, infopath.exe, msaccess.exe, mspub.exe, onenote.exe, outlook.exe, powerpnt.exe, steam.exe, thebat.exe, thunderbird.exe, visio.exe, winword.exe, wordpad.exe, notepad.exe.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (initial execution), the code enumerates and forcibly terminates a broad set of productivity, database, and email client processes using Windows API calls, ensuring files are not locked and maximizing the scope of file encryption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Killing user and business application processes is a hallmark of ransomware, as it ensures files are not in use and can be encrypted without errors.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not terminate unrelated user processes, especially productivity and database applications, as this disrupts user activity and data integrity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System maintenance tools may close specific processes for updates, but not such a broad and unrelated set of applications.
key_indicators: Targets a wide range of productivity, database, and email processes
Uses process termination APIs to forcibly close applications
Maximizes file encryption coverage by ensuring files are not in use

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (pre-encryption), the code executes the system command 'vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet' to silently delete all Volume Shadow Copies, removing backup snapshots and inhibiting system recovery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deleting all shadow copies without user interaction is a classic ransomware anti-recovery technique, preventing victims from restoring their files.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not delete all system backups without explicit user consent, as this removes critical recovery options.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup management tools may prune old snapshots, but not all at once and not without user notification.
key_indicators: Silent execution of 'vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet'
Removes all Volume Shadow Copies in a single operation
Prevents file recovery via system restore

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Encrypts files and appends .RAWLD or .yM8Yl extension to encrypted files.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (encryption phase), the code recursively enumerates user files, encrypts their contents using a cryptographic algorithm, and appends a unique extension (.RAWLD or .yM8Yl) to each encrypted file, rendering them inaccessible without the decryption key.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mass file encryption with a unique extension is the core behavior of ransomware, directly impacting data availability.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not encrypt user files in bulk without explicit user action and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encryption tools may encrypt files, but only with user initiation and clear notification, not automatically or indiscriminately.
key_indicators: Bulk file encryption across user directories
Appends unique extension (.RAWLD or .yM8Yl) to files
Files become inaccessible without a decryption key

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Drops ransom note 'Data breach warning.txt' with contact info, payment instructions, and a hardcoded list of unpaid victims.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (post-encryption), the code writes a ransom note file named 'Data breach warning.txt' to disk, containing extortion instructions, attacker contact information, payment details, and a hardcoded list of other unpaid victims to increase psychological pressure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping ransom notes with payment instructions and victim lists is a defining feature of ransomware, serving both extortion and intimidation purposes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not extort users or demand payment for file access, nor does it display lists of other victims.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate software drops ransom notes or demands payment for file restoration.
key_indicators: Creation of ransom note file with payment instructions
Inclusion of attacker contact info and victim lists
File named 'Data breach warning.txt' appears after encryption

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Steals files (design drawings, legal documents, management emails, financial documents, other files) and uploads them to attacker-controlled sites (Gofile, .onion leak site).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (pre-encryption, exfiltration phase), the code enumerates and collects sensitive files such as design drawings, legal documents, management emails, and financial documents, then uploads them via network connections to attacker-controlled servers, including public file sharing (Gofile) and .onion leak sites, enabling double extortion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating sensitive data before encryption is a double extortion tactic, increasing leverage over victims by threatening public exposure.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not upload sensitive files to unknown or attacker-controlled servers without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Cloud backup tools upload files, but only to trusted, user-configured destinations with clear user consent.
key_indicators: Bulk exfiltration of sensitive documents
Network connections to public file sharing and .onion sites
Data transfer occurs before file encryption

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Creates mutex: 'For whom the bell tolls, it tolls for thee.'
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime (initialization), the code creates a uniquely named mutex ('For whom the bell tolls, it tolls for thee.') using Windows API calls to ensure only one instance of the ransomware runs on the infected system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of a unique, contextually significant mutex string is a common malware technique to prevent reinfection and track execution, and the string itself is highly unusual.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software may use mutexes for instance control, but typically uses generic or product-related names, not literary or contextually suspicious phrases.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate applications use mutexes to prevent multiple instances, but the mutex name is usually product-specific and not a literary reference.
key_indicators: Creation of mutex with unique, suspicious string
Mutex used to control malware instance execution
String 'For whom the bell tolls, it tolls for thee.' is not associated with legitimate software

attack_chain.action: Malware executes and creates a unique mutex to ensure only one instance runs.
Terminates security, backup, and productivity services and processes to disable protection and maximize file access.
Deletes all Volume Shadow Copies to prevent system recovery.
Steals sensitive files and uploads them to attacker-controlled servers.
Encrypts user files and appends a unique extension.
Drops ransom note with extortion instructions and a list of unpaid victims.
attack_chain.leads_to: End of attack chain (awaits victim response)

behavioral_signatures: Mass termination of security, backup, and productivity processes/services using Windows API calls
Execution of 'vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet' to remove all Volume Shadow Copies
Bulk file encryption with unique extension (.RAWLD, .yM8Yl) across user directories
Creation of ransom note file named 'Data breach warning.txt' with extortion instructions and victim list
Exfiltration of sensitive files to public file sharing (Gofile) and .onion leak sites prior to encryption
Creation of unique mutex with suspicious string 'For whom the bell tolls, it tolls for thee.'
file_indicators: Files with .RAWLD or .yM8Yl extension in user directories
Presence of 'Data breach warning.txt' ransom note in affected folders
Mutex named 'For whom the bell tolls, it tolls for thee.' created in system
network_indicators: Outbound connections to .onion domains via TOR network
Unusual outbound traffic volume during or immediately after process/service termination and before file encryption
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for mass termination of security, backup, and productivity processes/services via Windows API calls. Alert on execution of 'vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet' and the sudden removal of all Volume Shadow Copies. Detect bulk file modifications with new extensions (.RAWLD, .yM8Yl) across user directories. Watch for creation of ransom note files named 'Data breach warning.txt' containing extortion instructions and victim lists. Monitor for outbound connections to gofile.io and .onion domains, especially during the pre-encryption phase. Correlate these behaviors with the creation of a mutex named 'For whom the bell tolls, it tolls for thee.' to identify RA World ransomware activity.
